summary: Astronaut Health Monitor is an interactive prototype that connects personal health information with the spacecraft environment. Personal mode provides nine health indicators, readable trends and measurement explanations. Ship mode shows six selectable modules with automatically simulated cabin conditions and crew movements. Crew members can dictate or type a wellbeing note, review the text and confirm it. Each entry preserves the available measurements, module context and source quality. Prepared rules explain possible temporal associations and missing evidence without assigning a diagnosis. Source-linked Help, daily wellbeing check-ins and an incident timeline support review. Users can download a JSON report, with private transcripts included only by choice. NASA resources informed the mission context and measurement categories. Telemetry is synthetic, browser dictation may require internet, and the prototype has no real spacecraft integration or flight-medical approval.
details:
THE PROBLEM

During a space mission, a measurement is useful only when the crew can understand its context, recognise missing information and find an appropriate next step. Sleep, daily activity and personal wellbeing also matter alongside vital signs.

OUR SOLUTION

Astronaut Health Monitor connects a visual overview, detailed measurements, prepared assistance and a daily routine.

Status uses a gently flowing sphere with a short explanation of the selected demonstration state. Health provides nine indicators: heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, temperature, systolic and diastolic pressure, sleep, activity and wellbeing. Minute views retain frequent samples; daily views show the last available reading of each UTC day. Explanations describe measurement methods and limitations.

Ship mode connects personal observations with the crew’s surroundings. Six selectable modules display synthetic cabin conditions and automatically simulated crew positions. The interface distinguishes fresh, stale and missing environmental data from the availability of crew-position information.

Voice check-ins let a crew member dictate or type how they feel, correct the text and confirm the entry. The saved record preserves its UTC confirmation time, available personal measurements, module conditions and recent simulated presence. History and Help show the recorded context, supporting evidence and missing information. The current association logic demonstrates a prepared Habitat A example.

Help provides prepared questions and quick replies for sensor issues, symptoms, collapse and routine review. Sources accompany the messages. No language model generates medical instructions at runtime.

Daily plan supports an illustrative activity day or a recovery day, measurement review and a three-question check-in. The user records energy, an optional reflection and their own wellbeing rating. That rating updates Health for today. Completed tasks earn a calendar mark regardless of whether the wellbeing rating is high or low.

Connection prepares a downloadable JSON report with selected measurements, history and optional check-in notes. It does not transmit messages.

NASA RESOURCES AND ORIGINAL APPROACH

NASA Human Research Program resources informed the mission-health context. NASA medical-standard material informed the vital-sign categories. Mission-operations resources helped frame prepared crew assistance and communication constraints.

Our approach connects confirmed personal observations with synthetic module conditions, recent simulated crew presence and source quality. A prepared Habitat A example shows how shared crew observations can support review while keeping the cause uncertain. The visual overview, prepared assistance and downloadable incident report make this context accessible to the crew.

IMPLEMENTATION AND SCOPE

We used React, TypeScript, CSS and a procedural WebGL sphere. Daily records are stored locally in the browser.

Measurements are synthetic, and scenario states are selected for demonstration. The prototype has no real sensor integration, validated diagnostic engine or approved flight emergency checklist. Real medical use would require specialist review and validation.

Browser speech recognition may use an online service provided by the browser vendor. The app stores confirmed text rather than audio. Offline onboard recognition and real spacecraft adapters remain future integration work. Private transcripts and their context enter an exported report only when the user explicitly selects them.

OpenAI image generation was used for the space background and background removal from the spacecraft illustration.
